reasoning: 4-year-old with altered mental status (unresponsive) following near-drowning with aspiration risk
Recent out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation by bystander indicates cardiac arrest or severe respiratory compromise occurred
Persistent unresponsiveness despite spontaneous breathing is a critical red flag for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, cerebral edema, or ongoing tissue hypoperfusion
Vital signs show tachycardia (HR 126, age-appropriate upper limit ~130 but elevated for resting state) and tachypnea (RR 28, normal for age ~20-30 but at upper range suggesting compensatory effort)
BP 80/64 is LOW for a 4-year-old; normal systolic for age is 95-105 mmHg; hypotension suggests shock state or inadequate cerebral perfusion
SpO2 96% on non-rebreather is marginally acceptable but does not rule out ongoing cellular hypoxia or pulmonary edema from aspiration
Altered mental status alone with high-risk mechanism (drowning) mandates ESI-1; unresponsive state requires immediate intervention

Immediate life-saving interventions needed: airway protection assessment, IV access, continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, possible ICU-level support for post-resuscitation care and cerebral edema management
red_flags: Unresponsiveness post-resuscitation (risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury)
Near-drowning with aspiration (risk of pulmonary edema, secondary drowning)
Hypotension relative to age (80/64 is below expected for 4-year-old)
Age <6 with altered mental status (unable to assess orientation/confusion directly but unresponsiveness is absolute marker)
SpO2 96% may be falsely reassuring if core tissue perfusion remains compromised
